He may demand. Beit Yosef writes that this applies not only where one lent one hundred for one hundred fifty, but even where monthly interest was stipulated.
To defer him. Shach writes that with an arev shaluf dotz, even interest already paid may be recovered from the Jewish guarantor, unlike Rama. Bach is still more lenient, but the authorities disagree. Shach understands the leniency of Rabbi Yosef Korkos as applying only to an arev kablan, not shaluf dotz.
To give. Taz writes that a borrower who agreed to reimburse all damages from late payment need not repay profits the lender pays to a third party, even through a permitted loan. Reimbursement of such financing costs is still interest. Taz also discusses partnership borrowing: if one active partner borrows from a non-Jew for the business, the interest may be treated as a partnership expense; if a passive investor borrows personally and contributes the funds, he may not shift that interest to the partnership.
Already. Taz disagrees with Rama and would recover interest already paid. Shach and Nekudot HaKesef uphold Rama. Taz permits paying a fee to an arev kablan because the fee compensates assumption of risk, not a loan. He forbids paying one who becomes the sole promissory-note obligor, though Nekudot HaKesef doubts this and notes lenient custom.

Or in any case, it is only as a guarantor for the interest, etc. Levush wrote: and some say that even without collateral — even if the non-Jew took the money directly from the lender — and even if the Jew became guarantor only for the interest — it is forbidden to be an arev kablan for the non-Jew, since when the Jew says to him "as long as my money is with the non-Jew I will give you a dinar per month," it follows that as long as the non-Jew does not pay, he is obligated to give the interest — and thus responsibility for the principal is also upon him until the non-Jew repays. Guarantor. Under their law the borrower may direct the lender to the guarantor, so it is as though the non-Jew lent to the guarantor and the guarantor lent to the borrower. Even without shaluf dotz this may create Jewish interest because the lender's money increases with the Jewish guarantor. Shach.
The principal. Taz questions Rama's implication that even an otherwise prohibited guarantor arrangement may be fulfilled as to principal. Nekudot HaKesef answers that merely becoming guarantor is not forbidden; only paying the interest is. Therefore principal may always be paid.
From his hand. Even without formal guarantee, if the Jew receives the money from another Jew he becomes the borrower, because a non-Jew has no halachic agency. If the Jew later pays interest, it is forbidden; if the non-Jew pays the interest directly, it is permitted. Shach.
Collateral. Levush discusses whether a Jew may guarantee only the interest where the non-Jew receives the funds directly. Shach distinguishes an explicit arrangement in which ongoing interest makes the Jewish guarantor effectively responsible for principal, which is forbidden, from a case with no principal liability, which is permitted. With adequate non-Jewish collateral, common practice permits a Jew to guarantee interest alone. See siman 169.
To pay. Shach writes that the lender need not first sue the borrower or non-Jewish guarantor. Where collateral was returned based on the guarantor's instruction, the guarantor must pay even without a kinyan, like a guarantor at the time of the loan. Whether release of a guarantor requires a kinyan remains uncertain, except an arev kablan is treated like the borrower himself.
From then onward. Taz writes that if the Jew made a kinyan, he must pay even future interest because a guarantor after the loan becomes obligated through kinyan. Shach cites Beit Yosef that even with kinyan he is exempt from interest accruing thereafter.

yad_avraham.he: (שם) ואם היה לישראל כו' ערב עובד כוכבי' ובא ישראל וא"ל למלוה שיפטור ערב העובד כוכבים והוא ערב לו צריך לשלם לו כל הרבית שעלה כו'. הטעם במרדכי בשם ראבי"ה שהישראל נכנס תחת הערב העובד כוכבים ובדיניהם היה הערב העובד כוכבים פורע תחילה. מש"ה גם הישראל שנכנס במקומו חייב לשלם. וצ"ע דאמאי סתם הג"ה האי דינא שהרי לפי מ"ש הרא"ש והטור והג"ה ר"ס זה דהאידנא נהגו גם הם בדיניהם שלא לתבוע הערב תחלה רק תובעין תחלה להלוה אם יש לו. ולפ"ז גם הישראל שנכנס תחת ערב העובד כוכבים א"צ לשלם תחלה אלא יכול לדחותו אצל הלוה וראבי"ה לטעמיה דס"ל כמ"ש הש"ע סימן זה בשם י"א דבדיניהם תובעין תחלה את הערב וכמ"ש הב"י והבאר הגולה שזהו דעת ראבי"ה: **** ENGLISH **** (There) And if Israel had gentile guarantor and Israel came told lender release gentile guarantor and he guaranteed must pay all ribbit accrued. Reason Mordekhai Rabeiah Israel entered under gentile guarantor their law gentile guarantor paid first; therefore Israel who entered his place must pay; tzaruch iyun why stam Hagah this law since Rosh Tur Hagah beginning this siman now practiced their laws not sue guarantor first only sue borrower first; therefore Israel entering under gentile guarantor need not pay first may push to borrower; Rabeiah to his reason holds as Shulchan Aruch this siman Yesh Im Mi their law sue guarantor first as Beit Yosef and Beer HaGolah Rabeiah's view.
yad_avraham.en: (Siman 170 seif 2 in Hagah) And if Israel guaranteed etc. For ribbit not principal permitted. Seems not every guarantee permitted unless accepts pay fixed amount entire loan duration; if accepts pay dinar monthly — also principal as Baal HaTerumot Beit Yosef siman 168 Bahat Halacha seif 13; likewise Taz siman 160 s.y. 3 brought there seif 13 and beginning siman 164; Beit Yosef and Shach this siman Bahat Halacha no distinction guarantor accepts fixed matter or dinar monthly — there explicitly guaranteed principal too heter because lender accepts not sue guarantor first therefore no distinction; where guaranteed ribbit alone permitted though sue guarantor first certainly permit only as I wrote; Bahat Halacha words do not contradict.
